topic: The Pi Mystery: Counting Collisions to Calculate Digits
target_audience: High school students or undergraduates with basic physics and geometry knowledge

sections.title: Introduction: The Impossible Counting Problem
sections.content: Introduce the setup: Two blocks on a frictionless surface. Block A (mass 1 kg) moves toward Block B (mass 100^N kg). How many total collisions occur before they stop moving toward each other? State the surprising link: the total number of collisions is the first N+1 digits of pi.
sections.example: Visualize a small mouse (Block A) running toward a massive elephant (Block B) on a frictionless icy pond.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly explain the tools needed: Conservation of Momentum and Conservation of Kinetic Energy. Explain that for perfectly elastic collisions, these two laws lock the velocities of the blocks into specific geometric relationships.
sections.example: An animation showing vectors for momentum (mass × velocity) and energy (0.5 × mass × velocity^2) balancing perfectly during a collision.

sections.title: Mapping Physics to Geometry: The Phase Space
sections.content: Introduce the 'Phase Space' concept. Map the velocities of Block A and Block B onto a 2D Cartesian plane (V_A on X-axis, V_B on Y-axis). Show how each collision acts as a 'reflection' against a barrier, creating a circular arc path.
sections.example: A visual animation showing the block velocities tracing a circular path (the 'arc') on a coordinate grid as they bounce back and forth.

sections.title: The Emergence of Pi
sections.content: Explain that the number of reflections is determined by the angle of the path hitting the 'walls' of the energy constraint. As the mass ratio increases (100^N), the path length matches the circular geometry required to reveal the digits of pi.
sections.example: A side-by-side comparison: a geometric circle drawn on a grid and the path of the blocks; as mass increases, the path segments perfectly 'measure' the curve of the circle.

sections.title: Conclusion and Summary
sections.content: Recap: Physics (conservation) turns into Geometry (billiards), which reveals Number Theory (pi). Emphasize that complex physical systems can act as an 'analog computer' for fundamental mathematical constants.
sections.example: Display a final table: N=0 (1 collision), N=1 (31 collisions), N=2 (314 collisions), N=3 (3141 collisions) leading to the value 3.141...
